title: Micron's NT$150 Billion Taoyuan Plant Reportedly Halted; Third Round of Labor Talks Set for Tomorrow
text:
Micron's NT$150 Billion Taoyuan Plant Reportedly Halted; Third Round of Labor Talks Set for Tomorrow — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers Micron's NT$150 Billion Taoyuan Plant Reportedly Halted; Third Round of Labor Talks Set for Tomorrow
 Add preferred source Micron has reportedly suspended nearly all construction work on its new Fab 11E facility in Taoyuan due to an unresolved labor dispute. The project carries an investment budget of approximately $4.5 billion (about NT$150 billion) and was originally scheduled to begin production in 2028, with plans to manufacture HBM and DRAM. Micron said in a statement that its Taiwan operations remain normal and that it is confident in safeguarding customer business continuity, but it did not directly address the Taoyuan plant. Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs said it will continue to provide assistance, while Taiwan's Ministry of Labor noted that both sides will hold a third round of negotiations tomorrow. Taiwan accounts for roughly 60% of Micron's global DRAM output, and how this case unfolds will ripple through the AI memory supply chain. Key Elements 
 Micron Taoyuan plant Fab 11E ASML Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs Taiwan's Ministry of Labor Taoyuan City Government High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) DRAM Taichung Union Taoyuan Union Memory chip giant Micron's plan to invest approximately $4.5 billion (about NT$150 billion) in a new memory chip plant in Taoyuan has reportedly ground to a near-total halt due to a prolonged labor dispute. According to Bloomberg, people familiar with the matter said Micron has notified Taiwanese officials and a supplier that construction at the Taoyuan plant is being suspended. Company executives are concerned that an agreement reached with the local union could be overturned. Only limited safety and maintenance work remains at the site, and construction will be frozen once that work is completed.
 The new facility, known as Fab 11E, was originally scheduled to begin production in 2028, with plans to use advanced ASML equipment to manufacture high bandwidth memory (HBM) and DRAM. Micron budgeted between $3 billion and $4.5 billion for the project, including spending on ASML equipment. Because HBM and DRAM are indispensable components for Nvidia accelerators and AI data centers worldwide—and market supply is extremely tight with prices surging—news of the disruption at the Taoyuan plant adds further uncertainty to an already strained memory supply chain.
 In response to media reports of the suspension, Micron said in a statement that Taiwan plays an important role in its global footprint, that operations are currently proceeding as normal, and that "we are confident in safeguarding our customers' business continuity." The statement did not directly address questions about the Taoyuan plant.
 The labor dispute was triggered by employees demanding a share of the record profits generated by the AI business. The Taoyuan Union argues that Micron should distribute 15% of operating profit to employees worldwide and wants the rewards paid entirely in cash rather than partly in stock. In October, Micron reached an agreement with the Taichung Union—the larger of the two unions—to raise employee compensation, but some employees remain dissatisfied with the terms. The Taoyuan Union is seeking to expand its membership in order to push for renegotiation.
 Regarding the regulatory authorities, Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs said in response that Micron has long been deeply invested in Taiwan, with cumulative investment reaching NT$1.6 trillion (approximately $48.5 billion) and about 15,000 employees in Taiwan, making it one of Taiwan's most important foreign investors and a key industrial partner in the AI era. The government understands that the two sides differ on compensation systems, but initial progress has been achieved through negotiations. The Ministry of Economic Affairs will work with Taiwan's Ministry of Labor and local government to help both sides continue communicating, balancing employee rights with corporate sustainability. The ministry also emphasized that the status of individual plant construction and follow-up plans should be based on the company's public statements.
 Taiwan's Ministry of Labor noted that to properly handle the labor dispute at Micron's Taoyuan plant, the Taoyuan City Government's Department of Labor had previously assisted both sides in two rounds of negotiations, with the Ministry of Labor sending personnel to participate and provide assistance. The two sides have scheduled a third round of negotiations for tomorrow (the 6th), and the Ministry of Labor will send representatives to attend and continue helping to build consensus. The Taoyuan City Government said it has not yet received notice from Micron of a construction suspension but hopes Micron and its employees can reach a consensus.
 In terms of industry standing, although the Taoyuan plant is not Micron's largest facility in Taiwan, it is a flagship investment. Taiwan currently accounts for roughly 60% of Micron's global DRAM output and is also an important production base for its HBM. Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan and has invested nearly $50 billion (about NT$1.6 trillion) over the past 30 years, making it Taiwan's largest foreign investor. Should Micron scale back its investment in Taiwan, it would be a major blow to Taiwan's semiconductor cluster.
 The market's focus is on whether this suspension is a short-term bargaining chip in the labor standoff or the opening move in Micron's reassessment of its Taiwan expansion plans. As demand for HBM from AI servers continues to climb, the capacity Micron's Taoyuan plant was set to bring online in 2028 coincides with the next wave of AI data center buildouts. A prolonged construction halt could not only affect Micron's competitive pace in the HBM market against South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, but could also prolong the global memory supply shortage.
 For investors, two indicators bear watching in the near term: first, whether tomorrow's third round of labor negotiations yields substantive progress; second, whether Micron adjusts its capital expenditure plans in upcoming earnings reports or earnings calls. Analysts believe Micron's Taiwan investment affects the upstream equipment, materials, and packaging and testing supply chains. If the suspension drags on, order visibility for related Taiwanese companies could be affected, but if the labor dispute is resolved in the near term, the impact on the broader AI supply chain is expected to remain limited.
